title: Hybrid Quantum-Classical Algorithm For Robust Optimization via Stochastic-Gradient Online Learning
abstract_summary: This preprint generalizes the Ben-Tal et al. online robust optimization meta-algorithm to allow stochastic subgradient oracles and develops a hybrid quantum-classical implementation. By using quantum state preparation, ℓ1-norm estimation and multi-sampling of subgradient entries, the method can reduce calls to subgradient and projection oracles and achieve up to quadratic improvements in problem dimension under suitable ℓ1/ℓ∞ norm conditions. The approach is applied to robust linear and semidefinite programs with example applications in finance (robust portfolio optimization) and engineering (truss design).
methodology_description: This is a theoretical and algorithmic study that generalizes the oracle-based online robust optimization meta-algorithm of Ben-Tal et al. (2015) to allow stochastic subgradients and to introduce a hybrid quantum-classical implementation. The authors formalize an input model with a noise memory (classical/quantum access) and define three oracles: a subgradient oracle (classical O∇ or quantum Q∇), a projection oracle OP onto the uncertainty set U, and an optimization oracle Oϵ for the original (non-robust) problem. They replace exact subgradient computation with a stochastic subgradient oracle Og that returns random vectors whose expectation is proportional to the true subgradient (up to a multiplicative factor bounded by ν). They first adapt online stochastic (sub)gradient descent and derive regret bounds for the noisy oracle setting. Building on that, they present two meta-algorithms: (i) a deterministic/stochastic dual-subgradient meta-algorithm (Algorithm 2) that uses Og and the optimization oracle Oϵ and (ii) a hybrid quantum-classical sampling-based dual-subgradient meta-algorithm (Algorithm 3). The hybrid approach uses quantum subroutines (quantum state preparation / multi-sampling from an ℓ1-weighted superposition and quantum ℓ1-norm estimation as in Hamoudi et al.) to produce ℓ1-sampled indices from the concatenated vector of all subgradient entries, and constructs a stochastic estimator g_i from counts and signs of sampled entries normalized by an estimated ℓ1 norm. At each iteration the algorithm: (a) samples s index pairs (i,j) in superposition proportional to |(∇_u f_i(x,u))_j|, (b) estimates the total ℓ1 norm of the concatenated subgradient vector, (c) forms sparse stochastic subgradients from the sampled entries and their signs, (d) updates each affected noise vector via a projected stochastic gradient step using OP, and (e) queries the optimization oracle Oϵ to obtain x for the next round. The paper proves correctness (probabilistic 3ϵ-approximate solution or correct infeasibility), derives iteration counts T and step sizes in terms of problem constants (D, F, G2, G1, G∞, ν, ϵ, δ), and provides detailed complexity bounds showing conditions under which quadratic speedups in the number m of noise vectors and/or the noise dimension d can be achieved. The methodology is purely algorithmic and analytical: algorithms are specified, oracles and input models are formalized, quantum subroutines are invoked as black-box primitives, and theoretical runtime and error analyses (lemmas and theorems) are provided. The authors also apply the algorithms analytically to robust linear programs and robust semidefinite programs with ellipsoidal uncertainty and derive specialized complexity expressions for those classes.

results_summary: This theoretical preprint generalizes an existing online oracle-based robust optimization meta-algorithm to the stochastic subgradient setting and constructs a hybrid quantum-classical variant that leverages quantum state preparation, ℓ1-norm estimation, and quantum multi-sampling to build sampled stochastic subgradients. Under assumptions about ℓ1 and ℓ∞ bounds on constraint subgradients (G1 and G∞), the hybrid method provably preserves approximation guarantees (a 3ϵ-approximate solution with high probability) while potentially reducing the number of calls to subgradient and projection oracles. The claimed quantum benefit is at most quadratic in the number of noise vectors m and the noise dimension d under sparsity-like conditions; in dense/worst-case regimes no asymptotic advantage is claimed. The approach is instantiated for robust linear and semidefinite programs with ellipsoidal uncertainty and discussed in finance (robust maximum-return portfolio) and engineering (truss design) examples. All results are theoretical/complexity claims (no experimental/empirical validation is provided).

No empirical demonstrations are provided; the advantage requires QRAM-style access, quantum state-preparation and sampling subroutines, and holds only in problem instances meeting the stated norm conditions (dense worst-case instances yield no asymptotic improvement).

Author-stated: The quantum advantage depends critically on the quantities G1 and G∞ (bounds on ℓ1- and ℓ∞-norms of subgradients). If G1G∞ = Θ(md G2^2) (dense instances) then there is no asymptotic quantum advantage.

Author-stated: The speedup is instance-dependent and occurs only for settings with favorable sparsity or ℓ1/ℓ2 structure (e.g., sparse sensitivity across constraints or entries). Dense inputs are not accelerated.
Author-stated: The algorithm assumes access to several oracles (quantum subgradient Q∇, classical projection OP, optimization Oϵ) and its runtime depends on their (possibly large) costs T∇, TP, Tϵ.
Author-stated: The projection cost TP can be large depending on the geometry of the uncertainty set U (e.g., polytope projections or certain ellipsoid/constraint projections with high complexity).
Author-stated: Robust semidefinite programs can be NP-hard in general (even with ellipsoidal uncertainty), so the framework provides approximate solutions and does not circumvent inherent hardness.
Author-stated: The algorithm returns a 3ϵ-approximate solution (constant-factor slack compared to ϵ), and requires a stochastic-subgradient oracle with specified moment bounds and variance control.

#idea:hybrid-approach — The hybrid algorithm interleaves sampled sparse subgradient updates (projected stochastic gradient steps using OP) with classical optimization-oracle queries Oε to produce iterates in the robust online meta-framework.

contradictions: The paper demonstrates that, within the Ben-Tal et al. meta-framework, only at-most-quadratic quantum speedups are plausible and that in worst-case norm settings the hybrid algorithm matches classical complexity — contradicting broader claims of large (e.g., exponential) quantum advantages for optimization tasks in finance.

The authors highlight that the asymptotic improvements depend on strong model assumptions (constant-time QRAM / noise-memory access and ideal quantum subroutines); this contradicts claims that quantum algorithms for optimization are practically scalable without addressing data-encoding/QRAM costs and realistic hardware constraints.
